title: Precedent and Interpretation
text:
In common-law systems, judges often rely on precedent when deciding a case. The doctrine of stare decisis requires courts to follow earlier rulings from higher courts that address materially similar facts. However, a court may distinguish a precedent when the facts of the present dispute differ in a meaningful way. This flexibility allows the law to evolve without abandoning its stability.

Critics argue that excessive reliance on distinguishing can undermine predictability, since litigants may never be sure which rule will govern their conduct. Supporters respond that rigid adherence to outdated decisions can produce unjust outcomes that no legislature intended. The tension between these positions is rarely resolved by abstract principle alone. Instead, it is settled case by case through careful analysis of the reasons underlying each earlier ruling.

questions.text: According to paragraph one, when may a court distinguish a precedent?
options: When the facts of the present dispute differ in a meaningful way
When the earlier ruling came from a lower court
When the legislature has explicitly repealed the statute
When both parties agree to ignore the earlier case

questions.text: According to paragraph two, what do critics of excessive distinguishing argue?
options: It can undermine predictability for litigants
It always leads to unjust outcomes
It causes legislatures to refuse to act
It removes the need for judicial reasoning

questions.text: What can be inferred about the author's view of stare decisis?
options: The author sees it as a principle that balances stability with adaptation
The author believes it should be abolished entirely
The author thinks courts should never consider the facts of a case
The author considers it useful only in criminal law

questions.text: What does the passage imply about resolving the tension between predictability and justice?
options: It depends on careful reasoning about the purposes behind earlier rulings
It can be settled once and for all by a single general principle
It is best left entirely to legislatures
It should be decided by the litigants themselves

to show that a earlier case does not apply because its facts are different
the quality of remaining steady and not changing suddenly
the quality of being possible to foresee what will happen
people or parties who are involved in a lawsuit

paragraph_translations: En los sistemas de common law, los jueces suelen basarse en el precedente al decidir un caso. La doctrina del stare decisis obliga a los tribunales a seguir las resoluciones anteriores de tribunales superiores que aborden hechos materialmente similares. Sin embargo, un tribunal puede distinguir un precedente cuando los hechos de la controversia actual difieren de forma significativa. Esta flexibilidad permite que el derecho evolucione sin renunciar a su estabilidad.

Los críticos sostienen que un recurso excesivo a la distinción puede socavar la previsibilidad, ya que los litigantes nunca pueden estar seguros de qué norma regirá su conducta. Los defensores responden que la adhesión rígida a decisiones anticuadas puede producir resultados injustos que ningún legislador pretendió. La tensión entre estas posturas rara vez se resuelve solo con principios abstractos. En cambio, se zanja caso por caso mediante un análisis cuidadoso de las razones que subyacen a cada resolución anterior.
